newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices firm on Iraq delays, grains and gold fall.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices firm on Iraq delays, grains and gold fall.

text.p: Oil prices closed higher on Friday as traders shrugged off doubts about whether major OPEC oil producers will be able to restrain oil sales and focused on more immediate delays in shipments by Iraq.
In other markets, corn prices fell to two-year lows on excellent growing weather in the Midwest and gold prices hit their lowest level in more than four years.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for August delivery closed 37 cents a barrel higher at $19.46. July unleaded gasoline ended 1.12 cents a gallon higher at 57.91 cents and July heating oil 1.31 cents higher at 53.33 cents.
On Thursday, Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz blamed the United States for blocking full implementation of an oil-for-food accord with the United Nations.

Under the deal, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq that have been in place since the Gulf War and allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months on a renewable basis to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian aid.
Iraq was to start its second six-month period on June 8, but oil sales have been held up until technicalities surrounding the distribution of aid are resolved.
"I am more confident than ever that we will see the resumption of Iraqi oil exports a little later than expected," said William Brown of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co.
"It may or may not be in July, depending on how the U.S. responds to the aid distribution plan submitted by Iraq," he said.

Oil prices had fallen sharply on Thursday after the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries decided to keep its ceiling on oil exports unchanged at 25.03 million barrels a day. Chronic quota-busting by OPEC members has pushed output to around 27 million barrels in recent months.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices fell to two-year lows and soybean and wheat prices also fell as near-ideal weather continued in the Midwest and Plains.
Corn for July delivery fell 4 cents a bushel to close at $2.46-1/4, the lowest closing price since April 1995. July soybeans closed at $7.87, down 13-1/2 cents a bushel.

Recent warm temperatures and showers have boosted prospects for those crops, already projected to achieve production at or near records this year. A heat wave expected next week should present no threat, analysts said.

"The feeling is there is a very high confidence level that the rain that is forecast will occur," said Dan Cekander, grain analyst for FIMAT Futures. "The weather guys have been forecasting rain and that has happened and there are some heavy rains in the forecasts."

Wheat for July delivery fell 7-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $3.25-3/4 as rapid harvest progress is expected over the next few days in Kansas and other key states where winter wheat is now being cut.
Gold prices slumped to a four-and-a-quarter year low at $334.00 an ounce in bullion markets on Friday, leading other precious metals lower across the board, traders said.

"We've seen good Australian producer hedging this week, continued fund selling, and the execution of some stop-loss orders around $336 in the bullion market," said Credit Lyonnais Rouse's New York chief bullion dealer Scott Mehlman.
"With the Hong Kong market closed next week for a holiday, there aren't going to be the usual buyers around either, so gold prices will probably go lower still," he said.

Gold for August delivery at the COMEX in New York ended down $3.90 an ounce at $335.90, after seeing a new life-of-contract low at $335.20. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $334.30/80 per ounce, the lowest level since March 1993.
In the past 18 months, the price of gold has slid from a seven-year high at $417.70.
Gold bugs have been in hibernation recently as surging world equity markets, a strong U.S. dollar and low inflation have provided little incentive for investors to diversify into gold, analysts said.
In addition, the threat of further European central bank gold sales in preparation for European monetary union has overhung the market, after a sale of 300 tons of gold by the Netherlands in January.
Silver for September delivery at COMEX ended 6.5 cents lower at $4.725 an ounce.
